newsitem.title: PERU: Miners trapped alive three days after Peru quake.
newsitem.headline: Miners trapped alive three days after Peru quake.

text.p: At least two miners were still trapped deep inside a collapsed tunnel on Friday, three days after an earthquake devasted southern Peru, killing 14 people and injuring hundreds.

Using picks and shovels, a group of about forty miners and firefighters tried to dig down to the men stuck in the hillside gold mine at Guanillo near Nazca, 290 miles (460 km) south of the capital Lima.
"I continue to hear my workmates' voices. They are alive," Saturnino Fernandez told Reuters at the site. He said they likely had some food and water underground.
The trapped men signalled they were alive by banging rocks from inside the tunnel -- one of many low passageways carved haphazardly into the hillside by freelance miners.
"Twice we have got to where we thought the sounds were but we did not find them," said frustrated fireman Ricardo Larrea, after rescuers dug just eight yards (metres) in over 24 hours.

At several remote mines around Nazca, where six people died and 25,000 were left homeless after the quake, rescuers on Thursday dug out four men trapped after landslides. In the first few hours after the quake, villagers dragged out several others from collapsed tunnels.
The quake that shook southern Peru and rocked Lima for one minute, measured 6.4 on the open-ended Richter scale. Its epicentre was 165 miles (260 km) southeast of Lima.
Most of the 14 victims were killed by falling debris. One miner died and 10 more were seriously injured in Moyohauca, 375 miles (600 km) south of Lima, in the area of Arequipa.

Freelance gold miners in Peru -- Latin America's second largest producer -- account for about 40 percent of national output. Small family groups usually work the same mine, using primitive technology to carve out tunnels.
